newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: INTERVIEW - Dutch Ahold aims for the top.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Dutch Ahold aims for the top.

text.p: Dutch supermarkets group Ahold NV aims to continue its 1996 expansion path in order to become the world's biggest supermarket organization within five to ten years, the company's spokesman said.

"(CEO) Cees van der Hoeven has developed this (growth) vision. In 1996, we have laid a new foundation for the next five years," Hans Gobes, director of communications at Ahold, told Reuters in an interview.
Gobes said that although some of Ahold's competitors had the same ambitions, Ahold had the experience and know-how needed to realise its ambitions.
"You need knowledge and a certain (company) culture. Ahold, which has been active in the U.S. for 20 years now, has built up a culture of internationalisation," he said.
Gobes said that shareholders had confidence in the company and gave it the necessary credit because "we deliver on what we promise.
"There are no surprises with Ahold, we are applying our strategy," he said.
In terms of sales Ahold still trails supermarket giants such as Kroger of U.S. and Carrefour of France but is roughly equal in size to Sainsbury of Britain and Japan's Daiei.

The group foresees an annual net profit growth of some 10 percent in the Netherlands, 15 percent in the U.S., 25 to 35 percent in Portugal and the Czech Republic and the same range in South-East Asia and Brazil in the long term, he said.
Besides becoming the world's biggest supermarket organization, Ahold intends to become one of the biggest global food retailers.
"Including Stop & Shop, Ahold now has an annualised turnover of 40 billion (guilders). We will take optimal advantage of our volumes by doubling our turnover within five to ten years," Gobes said.
He said Ahold preferred to invest in countries with above average growth rates. "We don't intend to enter over-competitive markets," said Gobes, giving the examples of Germany and France.
He characterized Portugal, the Czech Republic, South America and South-East Asia as growth markets, adding that in southern Europe Italy could also be interesting for Ahold.
Ahold is now initiating a new system of knowledge-transfer, in which well established subsidiaries adopt newer units, joint ventures or countries as a whole.
"Albert Heijn gets China and Spain, Bompreco will be adopted by Stop & Shop, Malaysia and Singapore by Tops and Thailand by Giant," said Gobes.
Ahold's best practice principle, in which subsidiaries compared the ways they handle their different activities and opted for the most effective, had enormous advantages, said Gobes.
"This is one of Ahold's strengths. We don't have to re-invent the wheel every time. We can learn a lot from Stop & Shop on several fields."
He added that Ahold was extremely satisfied with the development of the American chain it acquired in July this year.

While Tops stores would be opened in South-East Asian countries where Ahold was now active in order to obtain a store brand recognition with a private label, Gobes said a second store format would also be introduced in the region.
"You will hear more about this the coming months," he said. Along with supermarkets, Ahold operates discount and hypermarket chains in other regions.
Gobes said later opening hours in the Netherlands had had a positive influence on turnover and would feed through to margins as different products were sold in the evenings.
"Ready-to-eat meals are a clear growth market. There is an enormous interest in it," he said.

"It strengthens our competitive position; we get back part of the market that fast food took away. With quality and a low price, you can rapidly attract the market and also obtain an interesting margin".
Ahold's Dutch stores intended in time to dedicate more square meters to ready-to-eat meals, he added.
-- Christine Lucassen, Amsterdam newsroom +31 20 504 5000
